title: Switching to E-Cigarettes After Quitting Smoking May Nearly Double Your Lung Cancer Death Risk, a 4.5-Million-Person Study Finds
excerpt: The largest study of its kind, published in Nature Medicine, tracked former smokers for five years and found that those who switched to daily vaping had a 56% higher lung cancer incidence and a 100% higher lung cancer death risk compared to those who quit completely.
body:
The reassuring narrative around e-cigarettes — that they are a safer bridge away from traditional smoking — has taken its most significant hit yet.

A landmark study published in *Nature Medicine* on June 8, 2026, tracked 4,524,895 adults with a history of conventional smoking through South Korea's National Health Screening Program. The researchers classified participants as current smokers, short-term quitters (under five years), or long-term quitters, and followed them through December 2023. The findings are sobering: former smokers who used e-cigarettes daily after quitting had a 56 per cent higher risk of developing lung cancer and double the risk of dying from it, compared to those who quit all nicotine products entirely.

## The Numbers

Over 24.2 million person-years of follow-up, the study recorded 35,887 lung cancer cases and 12,807 lung cancer-specific deaths. The risk elevation was consistent across both short-term and long-term quitters, dismantling the assumption that vaping is benign once a person has been smoke-free for several years.

For the high-risk subgroup — adults aged 50 to 80 — the picture was even starker. E-cigarette use after cessation was linked to a 91 per cent higher risk of developing lung cancer and a 92 per cent higher chance of dying from it.

"Although causality cannot be established," the authors wrote, "these findings suggest that e-cigarette use after smoking cessation may attenuate the benefits of complete cessation for lung cancer prevention."

## Why Vaping Isn't Chemically Benign

The study adds biological plausibility to a growing body of concern. E-cigarette aerosols contain formaldehyde, acrolein, and toxic metals including lead, nickel, and chromium — all classified as carcinogens or probable carcinogens. A separate case-control study from Ohio State University, also published this year, found that young adults under 50 who both smoked and vaped had a 13.8-fold increased risk of lung cancer, compared to 5.0-fold for those who only smoked.

Pulmonary adenocarcinoma — the most common form of lung cancer in non-smokers and light smokers — accounted for 72 per cent of early-onset cases in the Ohio State study. For this specific cancer type, the combined vaping-and-smoking risk was 3.7 times higher than smoking alone.

## The Indian Diaspora Context

For the 5.4 million-strong Indian diaspora in the United States, these findings arrive at a particularly relevant moment. India banned the sale of e-cigarettes in 2019 under the Prohibition of Electronic Cigarettes Act — one of the most sweeping anti-vaping measures globally. But that ban does not extend to the diaspora.

Studies from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention show that vaping rates among Asian American teenagers and young adults — including Indian Americans — have risen steadily since 2020, driven by social media marketing, flavoured products, and the widespread perception that vaping is "safer" than smoking.

The cultural dimension matters too. Smoking rates among first-generation Indian Americans are relatively low compared to the general US population. But second-generation Indian Americans are increasingly picking up e-cigarettes as their first nicotine product — not as a cessation tool, but as a primary habit. For this cohort, the Korean study's finding that *even post-cessation vaping* carries substantial cancer risk raises the question of what lifetime risk accumulates for those who start vaping without ever having smoked.

## What the Experts Are Saying

The findings do not mean that vaping is worse than continued cigarette smoking for those who cannot quit. The study's comparison was between *complete quitters* and *vapers who had already quit smoking* — the relevant question for anyone who has already stopped.

Public health experts are now recalibrating their messaging. "We can no longer frame e-cigarettes as a universally safer alternative," said Yeon Wook Kim, the study's lead author from Seoul National University. "For someone who has quit smoking, the best evidence now says: quit everything."

The UK's National Health Service, which has historically endorsed vaping as a smoking cessation tool, is also reviewing its guidance in light of a companion *Nature Medicine* editorial warning that "long-term health risks of e-cigarettes after smoking cessation" need urgent reassessment.

## The Bottom Line

If you have already quit smoking, the 4.5-million-person message is clear: don't pick up an e-cigarette. The lung cancer risk reduction that comes from quitting is real and significant — but vaping after cessation appears to erode it substantially. For parents of teenagers who vape, the Ohio State data on combined smoking-and-vaping risk is equally alarming. The "safer alternative" framing is losing its evidence base.

**Sources:** Kim et al., *Nature Medicine* (2026), DOI: 10.1038/s41591-026-04469-5; Bittoni et al., *Frontiers in Oncology* (2026), DOI: 10.3389/fonc.2025.1741978; Medical Xpress
